1:
Henry begins with the delay rather than the alarm. Israel had been a good while in Canaan and no great matters were effected, Jericho taken by a miracle, Ai by stratagem, Gibeon by surrender, so that Joshua's prudence was perhaps censured as slothfulness and want of spirit. Three answers are given. Canaan was not to be conquered in a day, for God had said he would drive out the nations by little and little, and he that believeth will not make haste. Joshua waited for the Canaanites to be the aggressors, so that their destruction might be the more justifiable before men as well as God, and they the more inexcusable for resisting after seeing what favour the Gibeonites had found. And it was to Israel's advantage that the kings should combine and be cut off at one blow: they meant to strengthen one another, God to gather them as sheaves into the floor.

On the king's name they converge. Ellicott sets Lord of Righteousness beside King of Righteousness and finds the likeness of the names good evidence that the Salem of Genesis was Jerusalem, adding that the title may have belonged to the king not only locally but as suzerain over the surrounding tribes. Henry supposes him perhaps a descendant of Melchizedek, and remarks that for all the goodness of his name he was an implacable enemy of the posterity of that Abraham to whom his predecessor had been so faithful a friend. Gill turns to the city, whose name he takes for the possession of Salem, noting the Jewish scruple about its spelling. Keil and Delitzsch carry its later history forward, allotted to Benjamin but bordering Judah, burnt after Joshua's death and rebuilt by the Jebusites whom Judah could not destroy, so that the upper town on Zion remained a Jebusite fortress until David took it.

Calvin explains the shape of the narrative, that what was said of the kings in general is now applied to one man, not because Adoni-zedek alone was afraid but because he stirred up the others and was the chief author of the war; the plural verb shows that all were of one mind, while some hung back from fear and he who stood nearer the danger called the rest to arms. Wesley agrees that he sent either as their superior or as nearest the danger and most forward in the work. Calvin adds the reasoning behind the target: they turned first on Gibeon both to make an example of men who had betrayed their country and to give their own soldiers confidence, having a fair pretext in punishing those who had preferred to sanction strangers rather than defend their neighbours.

Clarke sets out the campaign in summary before turning to the towns, giving the distance of each from Jerusalem and the later fortunes of Lachish. Ellicott identifies the sites so far as he can, Lachish remaining uncertain. On the standing of Gibeon the accounts differ: Clarke denies that it was royal in the strict sense and makes it a small but powerful republic governed by elders, since no Gibeonite king is ever mentioned and their own embassy named none; Ellicott takes the phrase to mean one of the cities of the kingdom and notes that Gibeon was afterwards the city of Saul; Wesley allows either that it was really royal or merely equal to one. Gill, Clarke and Wesley agree that the five are called Amorites by a wide use of the name, since the men of Jerusalem were Jebusites and those of Hebron Hittites, the Amorites being simply the most numerous and powerful of the tribes. Ellicott adds the striking fact that in all the wars of Canaan we never read of one direct attack upon Joshua, the Canaanites acting strictly on the defensive and every army that took the field being attacked before it ventured to attack him.
6:
Whether the appeal went out before the siege or during it is the first question. Gill reports the opinion that they sent only when already besieged, which would show faith in the God they now professed, but judges it unlikely both that they should defer so long, having heard of the muster at Jerusalem, and that messengers could pass a surrounding army; he therefore renders the verb as a pluperfect, they had sent. Calvin says the same more shortly, that the narrative is inverted, since the Gibeonites did not wait to be besieged but, seeing an army levied and expecting the first onset as the most hated of all, anticipated the attack and hastened to Joshua's protection. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the plea, that to slack the hand from a servant is to withhold help, and warn that the clause about the Amorites of the mountains is added of the chief part only and does not warrant the conclusion that all the towns named lay in the mountains of Judah; those Amorites were the strongest of all the Canaanites. Ellicott places them in the hill country south of Jerusalem. Wesley draws out the ground of the appeal in three parts, that Joshua was bound to protect them in duty as their master, by his own interest since they were now part of his possessions, and in ingenuity, because they had given themselves to him.

Henry makes the march an act of plain honesty. Joshua resolved to assist his new allies, which was generous and just, though the king of Jerusalem had probably expected him to abandon them as Canaanites, the rather because their league had been obtained by fraud; but Joshua knew that his promise to let them live obliged him not only not to slay them himself but not to stand by and see them slain when it was in his power to prevent it. Gill notes that he went up because Gilgal lay low in the plains of Jericho, and Keil and Delitzsch that the verb is ascended rather than went, the men of valour being named by way of explanation rather than as a second body. Wesley takes the mighty men for an army of the most valiant picked out from the rest, since Joshua would neither take so many hundred thousand as would hinder one another nor leave the camp undefended.

Whether the word from God came before the resolve or after it is the second question, and it is left open. Calvin says plainly that it is uncertain whether the Lord anticipated the movement and drew Joshua out of Gilgal before he had taken a step, or only confirmed him once his preparations were made; he thinks it likelier that Joshua did not rush forth without consulting God, since, having lately been chastised for excessive facility, he probably attempted nothing in this difficulty except by a divine command. Gill reasons the same way and adds the ground of the doubt, that the league had been obtained by fraud, so that Joshua might well hesitate; Wesley likewise holds that he asked advice of God first, which the form of the answer implies. Ellicott stands apart from the conjecture and states the pattern instead, that a distinct command is given for the beginning of this attack as for all the important steps in the conquest of Canaan. Keil and Delitzsch describe the assurance as renewed, this being the first time Joshua was to fight several allied kings at once, and Calvin adds that the Lord had respect to the wretched Gibeonites in not leaving them destitute of the help of his people, making Joshua confident of victory precisely that he might succour them.
9:
Clarke calls it a forced march by night over the eighteen or twenty miles from Gilgal to Gibeon, so that the kings were confounded by an attack they had not looked for; Keil and Delitzsch reckon the distance at fully fifteen miles, all covered in a night. Ellicott corrects the rendering, the sense being that Joshua came upon them suddenly because all the night he had been marching up from Gilgal, and observes that the verb of ascent is geographically exact, the line of march being an ascent the whole way. Gill says only that the suddenness threw them into consternation. Wesley draws the lesson: though assured of the victory Joshua uses all prudent means, and it is not said that he covered the ground in a night's space but only that he travelled all night; for God's promises are intended not to slacken but to quicken our endeavours, and he that believeth does not make haste to anticipate providence, but does make haste to attend it, with a diligent and not a distrustful speed.

Keil and Delitzsch take the confusion as the fulfilment of an old promise in Exodus, produced, they judge from what follows, by thunder and lightning; the pursuit went by the ascent of Upper Beth-horon, nearest to Gibeon, on a promontory between two valleys and divided from the lower town by a long steep pass. Clarke has multitudes falling in the first onset before the rest fled, notes that there were two cities of the name, both in Ephraim and built by Sherah the daughter of Ephraim, and places Azekah and Makkedah in Judah. Gill describes the descent toward Azekah as a very narrow passage of which Josephus makes mention, and reports the Jewish tradition that this was where Sennacherib's army fell; Wesley notes that the slaughter was in the territory of Gibeon rather than in the city.

Calvin uses the two slaughters to settle a question of agency. In the first the Lord exerted his own might but used the swords of the people, from which we infer that when he works by men nothing is detracted from his glory: he does not call in allies as a subsidiary force, but, being able to accomplish whatever he pleases by a mere nod, uses men as instruments to show that they are ruled by his hand and will, so that it is equally true to say that the enemy were crushed by God or by the Israelites. In the second the hand of God appeared more clearly, the text stating expressly that more died by the hail than by the sword, so that no doubt might remain.

What fell is disputed. Clarke reports the contention that common stones are meant and that the word hail marks only the speed and quantity of their fall; he grants that stones have fallen from the clouds in many countries, that he owns fragments himself and that pieces may be seen in the British Museum, and that God might certainly have cast such stones down; yet he judges it likelier that hailstones in the proper sense are intended. Keil and Delitzsch agree, calling them hailstones and not a shower of stones, a terrible storm in which the hail fell in pieces as large as stones and killed more than the swords of Israel, manifestly miraculous since the stones slew the enemy without injuring the Israelites who pursued them. Wesley agrees and adds from Josephus that thunder and lightning were mixed with the hail. He closes with the irony of it: they had robbed the true God of his honour by worshipping the host of heaven, and now the hosts of heaven fight against them; Beth-horon lay north and Azekah and Makkedah south, so that they fled each way, but which way soever they fled the hailstones pursued them, and there is no fleeing out of the hands of God.
12:
Gill reads the first clause as prayer, Joshua entreating that sun and moon might stand still until the victory was complete, and records that the Jewish writers make it a song instead, the Targum having that Joshua then praised, a reading Jarchi and Kimchi approve. Calvin meets the difficulty head on. Some take the words to mean that he spoke of Jehovah rather than to him, since addressing God seems little in accordance with the modesty of faith and the next clause has Joshua speaking to the sun. Calvin has no doubt that the first clause denotes a prayer and the second an expression of confidence after he had been heard, for to command the sun without leave already obtained would have been presumptuous: he consults God first, and having his answer boldly commands the sun to do what he knows is pleasing to God. Keil and Delitzsch put it more plainly, that in reliance on the promise already given Joshua prayed during the battle that the Lord would not let the sun go down till Israel had taken vengeance, and the Lord hearkened; Wesley adds that he was moved by zeal against God's enemies and by the motion of God's Spirit, and spoke before the people so that they might be witnesses.

Wesley denies that the two places fix the two lights, as though the sun stood over one and the moon over the other, which is absurd when they lie so near together; the doubling is partly a poetical variation and partly a note of the line of pursuit from Gibeon toward Ajalon, the moon being asked to stay not because her light was needed but that the order of the heavens might not be broken. Calvin agrees that Joshua did not subtly fix the sun in a point, so that there is no need to feign a battle fought at the summer solstice: as it was turning toward Ajalon so far as the eye could reach, he bids it rest above the horizon, and the sun, already declining westward, is kept from setting. Ellicott gives the words their literal force, the sun was silent and the moon stopped, and observes that the verb cannot mean to rise, which excludes the reading that Joshua wanted the sun kept from rising to finish a night attack.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the passage as a quotation, the victory having been celebrated in a war-song preserved in the book of the Righteous. Wesley says the book was written before Joshua wrote and is fitly cited here, but is now lost, not being canonical and so not preserved by the Jews with the same care. He takes the whole day for an artificial day between sunrise and sunset, that being the day Joshua needed.

Clarke sets out his method before his explanation. He takes it for granted that a miracle was wrought as nearly as circumstances admit in the manner recorded, and will look for no allegorical sense; he holds the received system of the universe to be genuine and to be the system of the Mosaic writings, with the sun at rest in the centre and the earth turning about him and about its own axis, so that the rising and setting of the sun is caused by the earth's motion, as a ball hung before a candle will show; and he holds the solar influence to be the cause of both motions, alterable by no power but that of God, who can nevertheless suspend or even annihilate secondary causes. Calvin will have none of the enquiry: the question how the sun stood over Gibeon is as unseasonably raised by some as unskilfully explained by others, and the rebuke falls with double force on those who explain the miracle away, among whom are some of the most distinguished Jewish rabbis, who allow no miracle but only something very like one.
14:
Gill guards the claim two ways. The comparison is not with natural days, such as the long days of the poles, but with miraculous ones; and as for Hezekiah's day, it is uncertain whether the ten degrees were hours or halves or quarters, and even if hours the return could add only ten and make a day of twenty-two; besides which the point is less the length of the day than the manner of it. Wesley answers the polar objection likewise, those days being long by the order of nature while this length was purely contingent and granted in answer to prayer. Calvin allows the parallel more room: the sun's course was afterwards changed as a favour to Hezekiah, so that it is not absolutely denied that anything similar was conceded to another, but the miracle is extolled as singular. Clarke says simply that there was no period in which the sun was kept so long above the horizon, and reports that some learned men have supposed the fable of Phaeton founded on this history, though he confesses he can see nothing in the pretended copy to justify the opinion. Ellicott holds the words meaningless unless the writer meant that a great miracle had really occurred, and compares the prophecy that the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun.

Over the clause about the Lord hearkening to a man Calvin is careful. He rejects as too harsh the rendering which makes the verb mean that God obeyed: though the Psalm says the Lord does according to the desire of his servants, it is better to avoid anything that seems to give a subordinate office to God. Wesley presses the sense without the word, that God altered the course of nature so that a man might have more time to destroy his enemies, and takes the following clause for the reason of that readiness, the Lord being resolved to fight for Israel in a more than ordinary manner.

The verse about the return divides them from the text as it stands. Clarke argues from the rest of the chapter that the army did not return until after the kings were hanged and their cities destroyed, notes that it is omitted by the Septuagint and the Anglo-Saxon and seems not to have stood in the hexaplar versions, and judges it an encumbrance where it stands; if genuine here, he would read Makkedah for Gilgal. Calvin says the same, that the verse is not in its proper place and is omitted by the Septuagint, since what follows is the end of the battle, the punishment of the kings and the encampment at Makkedah. Ellicott calls it a relation by anticipation in the words of the Book of Jasher, the immediate return that day having been to Makkedah. Wesley agrees that it was not on the same day but after the matters that follow, the same words being repeated later, and takes the sentence as closing the general account of the fight. Gill alone defends the order, that Joshua determined upon the return and prepared for it but was prevented by the news that the five kings were hidden in a cave, though he allows that the verse may be out of place or superfluous.

Henry reads the moment as a lesson in unfinished work. The five kings had made a brave appearance and were now routed, so that Joshua thought his work done and his army entitled to quarters of refreshment, and it was resolved to return to the camp until God should give orders to take possession; but he soon found he had more work cut out for him, since the victory had to be pursued if the spoils were to be divided, and he applied himself with renewed vigour, setting a guard over the kings and reserving them for another day of destruction.
16:
Gill marks the escape as itself providential: the five were neither killed by the hailstones nor slain by the sword but got away, being reserved for a more shameful end. Clarke thinks it very likely that the cave was a fortified place among rocks, of which there were many in different parts of Palestine. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the definite article, the cave in Makkedah. Wesley calls it a place of the greatest secrecy and adds that there is no escaping the eye or hand of God; the town itself was not yet taken, so the hiding-place lay in its territory rather than in the city. Gill supposes the news came to Joshua either from his own people or from inhabitants of the land in his interest.

The order about the stones is read as a piece of economy. Gill has them rolled up to keep the kings in until Joshua should have time to bring them out and deal with them as they deserved, and remarks that there was doubtless plenty of stone about the hill fit for the purpose; the same care appears in the next order, that the men were not to stay at the cave but, a guard being set, to go after the enemy with all celerity. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the outcome, that when the great battle and the pursuit were over and the enemy consumed, the remnant of them got into fenced cities. Wesley explains why that mattered, since men once inside their cities would recover strength and renew the war, and reads the assurance that God has delivered them as meaning the work will be easy, God having already done it to their hands. Ellicott stops over the rare verb for smiting the hindmost, which occurs only once elsewhere, and observes that the command to exterminate the Canaanites, general as it sounds, is limited in the giving by conditions of time and circumstance, since Israel was to destroy the nations which the Lord should first bring them in against and cast out before them.

Calvin faces the harder question raised by what follows. The enemy routed, Joshua is now at leisure to punish the kings; but in considering this the divine command must always be kept in view, since without it there would be boundless arrogance and barbarous atrocity in trampling on the necks of kings and hanging their dead bodies upon gibbets. They had lately been raised by divine agency to a sacred dignity and placed upon a royal throne, so that it would have been contrary to the feelings of humanity to exult in their ignominy had not God so ordered it; but since such was his pleasure it behoves us to acquiesce without presuming to inquire why.

On the return the accounts agree in fact and differ in reference. Gill takes the phrase for sound and well, not one killed or missing and, as the Latin has it, not one wounded, the army coming back in full number. Wesley has the pursuing party rejoining the body that had stayed with Joshua before Makkedah, since Joshua himself did not go with them. Where they part is over the clause about the tongue. Clarke refers it to Israel, holding that the whole transaction of that day had been carried on so evidently under the direction of God that there was not the least murmuring among them, nor cause for it, their enemies being wholly discomfited. Wesley refers it to the Canaanites, whose men of war could not find their hands and were besides so confounded that they could not move their tongues by way of insult, as they doubtless did when Israel was smitten at Ai; now they were silenced as well as conquered, and durst provoke Israel no more.
22:
Gill glosses the order simply, that the cave was opened by rolling away the great stones laid against it, and the five set before Joshua after he had passed sentence. Keil and Delitzsch name them by their cities and set out the sequence: Joshua called for all the men of Israel, directed the leaders of the army to set their feet upon the necks of the kings, and only then had them put to death and hanged until evening, their bodies being thrown at last into the cave in which they had hidden. Ellicott stops over the word for the captains, which occurs here for the first time and seems to mean the actual leaders rather than the official heads of the people, the men who had borne the brunt of the battle; having laboured, they deserved to see the fruit of their labour, and the act was well calculated to inspirit them and to fire them with courage for the battles still to come.

What the act signified is put four ways. Clarke calls it symbolic, a token not only of the present complete victory but of the approaching triumph over all their adversaries, which is the interpretation Joshua himself gives in the words that follow. Wesley denies that it was done out of pride or contempt and makes it a punishment of impious rebellion against their sovereign Lord, in pursuance of the curse of servitude due to that people, and a token to assure the captains that God would subdue the proudest of them under their feet. Calvin takes it as a triumph in the persons of the five over all the rest who remained, since Joshua exhorts his people to confidence just as if those who still stood unsubdued were already prostrate beneath them; by the treading down of a few the whole people were so elated that they looked with contempt on all the others as already overthrown, and in that we have a brighter display of the divine power, which could inspire such confidence for the future. Ellicott observes that the words of encouragement are the very words Jehovah had spoken to Joshua at the outset, except that the term for fear is the stronger one there, so that even ordinary fear is needless and alarm not to be thought of; Gill adds that the charge was not about the kings, who lay bound and could make no resistance, but about the enemies still to be met.

Over the hanging Clarke is careful to clear the practice. Hanging alive seems a barbarous custom, but among the Hebrews criminals were first deprived of life, which was the debt required by justice, and only then hanged up, perhaps generally by the hands rather than the neck, by way of example to deter others from the crimes for which they had suffered; and they were never permitted to hang all night, since that could answer no purpose either of justice or of example, the bodies not being visible in the dark. Ellicott agrees that the hanging here appears as a token of disgrace after death, and turns it forward, since upon the cross of the true Joshua the enemies of the Israel of God are exhibited and a show made of them openly. Calvin says likewise that the kings were hung up not for the purpose of exercising greater severity upon them. Gill notes that sunset was the time fixed by the law for taking down bodies that had been hanged, and Wesley that they were taken down so that neither wild beasts could devour them nor their own people give them honourable burial; and he closes on the shape of the whole episode, that what they thought would be their shelter was made their prison first and then their grave, so that we shall surely be disappointed in whatever we flee to from God.
28:
How much belongs to the one long day is the first question. Wesley takes the whole run of it, finding nothing strange in so much being done and places so far apart taken, when the day was so long and the Canaanites struck with such terror. Gill refers the phrase more narrowly to the day the five kings were hanged, noting that some make it the day the sun stood still. Clarke allows the first town only: Makkedah may well have been taken on the evening of the miraculous day, but the other cities were certainly subdued some days later, since an army exhausted by a whole night's march and two days' fighting could not have gone further that night. Ellicott suggests a pluperfect, that Makkedah had been taken before the execution of the kings. Keil and Delitzsch date the capture to the day of the impaling and describe the terms, the town and its king smitten with the sword, the inhabitants put to death under the ban, the cattle taken as booty as at Ai, and the king treated as the king of Jericho.

Henry praises the generalship: Joshua improved the victory he had won and the advantages it gave him, which is a commander's proper praise. Of the five kings' cities he took Lachish, Eglon and Hebron, though Jerusalem and Jarmuth were not taken then, his forces being perhaps too fatigued or too well satisfied with what they had. Calvin measures it by the difficulty: here are the cities out of which the enemy's army had been raised, and in taking them God displayed his power no less wonderfully than in the open field, especially when the rapidity is considered, for the men who fled into them might spread panic at first, but once the fear was allayed they could serve for defence, the garrisons being increased by their numbers.

On the towns themselves identifications and later histories are gathered. Keil and Delitzsch place Libnah among the towns of Judah, allotted to the priests, in revolt under Joram and besieged by Sennacherib, and look for it north-west of Lachish; Clarke sets it near Makkedah and adds that Sennacherib besieged it after being obliged to raise the siege of Lachish; Ellicott treats the operations there as the opening of a further stage of the campaign and admits that the site has not been identified. Gill gives the distances on Bunting's authority, and Ellicott lists the rival identifications of Lachish while allowing it cannot have been far from Eglon. Clarke observes that Lachish was anciently a very strong place, since for all the panic of the enemy Joshua could not reduce it until the second day; Ellicott connects the same two days with two later facts, that Sennacherib laid siege to it with all his power and had to abandon it, and that Jeremiah names Lachish and Azekah among the defenced cities of Judah still left when Nebuchadnezzar invaded. Gill notes that the second day may be reckoned either from the slaughter of the kings or, as Kimchi has it, from the beginning of the siege.

The last town brings a king into the field. Gill supposes Horam was the readier to come because Lachish had no king of its own, and observes that whether he arrived before the city fell or after, he was either unable to raise the siege or too late, and in both cases fell into Joshua's hands; in Jerome's time Gezer was a village four miles north of Nicopolis. Clarke thinks Horam was in alliance with Lachish and came as soon as it appeared his ally would be attacked, Joshua probably sending a detachment against him before he could effect a junction. Keil and Delitzsch note that nothing is said of the capture of Gezer itself, which by later notices remained in Canaanite hands, and Ellicott places it a few miles from Emmaus.
34:
Gill puts Eglon at eight miles from Lachish and twelve from Jerusalem to the south on Bunting's reckoning, and Clarke agrees that it cannot have been far from Lachish; Keil and Delitzsch have Joshua proceeding eastwards against it, taking the town and dealing with it as he had dealt with Lachish. On the speed of its fall Gill notes that they took it the same day they encamped and besieged it, the besieged finding themselves unable to hold it, and Wesley says simply that it fell on the day they first attempted it.

Hebron raises the one real difficulty of the section. Gill observes that the town lay in the hill country, so that they are said to go up to it from the lower ground of Eglon, sixteen miles away, and Keil and Delitzsch describe the same ascent from the lowland to the mountains, with the town, its king and its dependent villages treated as the others had been; but they add at once that the king of Hebron here cannot be the man already executed. Clarke states the problem without softening it: the earlier verses make the king of Hebron one of the five whom Joshua slew and hanged at Makkedah, so how can he be said to slay the king of Hebron when he took the city some days afterwards? Either the statement refers back to what had already been done, or else the Hebronites, finding their king had fallen in the battle, had set up another in his place, and it was this second king whom Joshua slew after the city was taken. Wesley notices that the conquest of Hebron is related here only in general and is afterwards repeated and described more particularly, and explains that the cities belonging to it were those under its jurisdiction, Hebron being a royal city like Gibeon and having towns dependent on it.

Debir is the last of them, and the least certainly placed. Ellicott says flatly that it has not been identified. Gill takes it for a city Joshua had passed by on his way to Hebron without fighting against it and returned to take once Hebron had fallen, and reports Bunting's estimate of a mile from Hebron and twenty-two from Jerusalem southward, though he doubts that figure at the next verse, since Debir was itself a royal city with others depending on it and must therefore have lain further off, Burchard making it five or six miles and another writer ten. He notes too that the place is the same as Kirjath-sepher and Kirjath-sannah, the city of a book or of books, that in Persian the name is said to carry the same sense, and that it was given from a library or from archives kept there. Wesley explains the word return differently, not as implying that Joshua had been there before, but because, having gone as far west and south as he thought fit, even as far as Gaza, he now turned back toward Gilgal, which lay to the north and east, and on the way fell upon Debir. Keil and Delitzsch have him turning southwards with the whole army and taking the town and its dependencies in the same manner as the rest, leaving none remaining, as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah before it. Over that formula Clarke alone hesitates: the words mean that they brought every person under an anathema, and he asks whether it is not reasonable to hold that those found in arms were slain while of the others they made slaves.
40:
Gill takes the summary for that part of Canaan which lay southward and consisted of hills and vales, abounding with springs and well watered, and observes that it answers the description Moses gave of a land he never saw. Ellicott identifies the four regions, the hills being the mountains of Judah and Ephraim, the south the Negeb, the vale the Shephelah or coastal plain though apparently not taking in the Philistine territory Joshua never conquered, and the springs a word some render slopes, the country between the high hills and the low plain. Wesley marks the limits instead, Kadesh-barnea in the south and Gaza in the south-west, so that Joshua subdued in this expedition all the parts lying south and west of Gilgal. Over Goshen the accounts divide. Wesley says shortly that it is not the Goshen of Egypt but another in Judah; Clarke reports that Calmet contends for the very country in which the Hebrews dwelt before leaving Egypt and has drawn his map accordingly, but thinks it plain that a city of that name in Judah gave its name to the neighbouring country; Ellicott admits the difficulty and refuses both answers, since it is inconceivable that a single place of no importance in the mountains of Judah should have named the extensive district manifestly meant here.

On the destruction Calvin sets out the whole ground of the defence. The divine authority is interposed again in order to acquit Joshua of any charge of cruelty, for had he proceeded of his own accord to an indiscriminate massacre of women and children, no excuse could have cleared him of a cruelty surpassing anything recorded of savage tribes scarcely raised above the brutes; yet what would otherwise horrify us justly, it becomes us to embrace with reverence as proceeding from God. Clemency is rightly praised as a principal virtue, but it is the clemency of men who moderate their wrath when injured and might have shed blood with justice; and since God had destined the swords of his people for the slaughter of the Amorites, Joshua could do nothing but obey. Wesley argues the same way, that the clause about the command vindicates the Israelites, whom God would not have suffer in their reputation for executing his orders, so that he acquits them of the cruelty they might be thought guilty of and takes it upon his own just indignation; and he reads the whole as a type of the final destruction of the impenitent enemies of the Lord Jesus. Clarke narrows the fact itself, holding that those destroyed were the persons found in arms who continued to resist, that those who submitted were spared, and that many escaped and afterwards reoccupied parts of the land.

The phrase about one time is taken by all to mean one campaign, not one day. Gill says it was not in a single day but in a very short time, as the history clearly shows; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the word as once, that is in one campaign, which nevertheless lasted a considerable while, and add that Joshua could accomplish it because Jehovah fought for Israel. Clarke calls that the rational construction of the Hebrew and presses the inference: the conquests were so rapid and stupendous that they cannot be attributed either to Joshua's generalship or to Israelite valour, and the author himself, disclaiming the merit, modestly and piously adds that the Lord fought for Israel, so that both reason and piety require the whole to be ascribed to God alone. Gill notes that the return took place only after all the kings and their cities had been taken, though the same words stood earlier, and Keil and Delitzsch bring the army back to Gilgal; Ellicott ends on the position itself, a central one, with Jordan and the conquered territory of the two and a half tribes in the rear.
